preamble: Raising of the close-mid front rounded vowel [ø] to the close [y]. In the vowel shift of Tatar and Bashkir, the Old Turkic mid vowels were raised to high and the old high vowels became a reduced mid series (Johanson 1998, as summarized by Wikipedia). Old Turkic *ö therefore became Tatar ү, as in *söz 'word' > süz, in parallel with *e > i (*et 'meat' > it) and *o > u (*sol 'left' > sul); Kazakh keeps söz, et and sol. Wikipedia's Tatar vowel chart places ү among the high vowels as [y~ʉ], while Wiktionary transcribes сүз as [sʏz]. Bashkir has the same development (*söz > hüź, transcribed [hyθ] in the comparison table of Wikipedia's Tatar article): Wikipedia's Bashkir phonology describes its non-reduced vowels as raised from mid to close, writes the result /ʏ/ (realized [ʏ̝]), and says the shift is less prominent in most Bashkir dialects than in Tatar. The old high vowel *ü moved the other way, to Tatar ө (y → ø).

examples.note: Old Turkic söz. Wikipedia's Tatar vowel chart gives ү as [y~ʉ]; Wiktionary transcribes сүз as [sʏz]. Kazakh keeps söz.
Bashkir has the same vowel in һүҙ 'word', күл 'lake' and дүрт 'four', which Wiktionary transcribes [hʏð], [kʏl] and [dʏrt].
